Eddy Cue testified in the US v. Google antitrust trial defending the Information Services Agreement (ISA), which has made Google the default search engine on Apple devices since 2002. In 2016, Cue negotiated the current iteration of the ISA with Google CEO Sundar Pichai; while Apple sought a higher revenue share and Pichai wanted to maintain the status quo, they compromised on an undisclosed percentage.

Cue argued there was no valid alternative to Google at the time and none exists now, stating Apple never seriously considered switching providers or building its own search product. He emphasized that the deal was about more than economics. Regarding user experience, Cue acknowledged the ISA did not allow Apple to offer search engine choices during setup, citing speed and user experience as reasons for defaulting to Google.

On privacy, Cue agreed Apple values user privacy and claimed Apple offers better privacy than Google, citing ISA provisions for login-free searches and anti-tracking measures. When questioned about the ISA's impact on Apple's profits, Bellshaw asked if it represented a significant portion; Cue replied that Apple does not view it that way because the platform's overall appeal makes the agreement successful. Schmidtlein led Cue through Safari's history, noting Google integration was a user interface innovation mentioned in pre-2003 promotional materials. Cue explained that before 2003, users had to type specific URLs to search, whereas Apple's system redirects non-URL text to search. Schmidtlein and Cue argued that Google helped Safari succeed as a great product and that switching search engines is easy, referencing Apple's deals with Yahoo and Bing. Finally, in response to DOJ questions about whether Google is the best search engine or simply pays the most, and what the market looks like without those payments, Cue stated Apple never considered these factors.

* [Google antitrust case: key facts and Google's defense](google-antitrust-case-key-facts-and-google-s-defense.md) - Overview of the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google, including CEO Sundar Pichai's testimony on default search engine deals, specific financial figures, and historical context regarding browser defaults.
* [Google Search dominance, data practices, and competitive challenges](google-search-dominance-data-practices-and-competitive.md) - An analysis of Google's market dominance, data collection scope, personalization capabilities, and the controversies surrounding its search manipulation and default status.

  hash: sha256:dfc5f14c1b3c2a3df519a7813998b5fa20dce2c2e625da9f36a7b424631a6cf1

---

Google Search faces scrutiny regarding its market dominance, data collection practices, and the fairness of its default status. Kent Walker argues Google is preferred because it is the best, not just the default, citing user choice in Mozilla and Windows scenarios. However, users frequently revert to Google after Mozilla set Yahoo as Firefox default and after Microsoft set Bing as default in 2021, indicating displacement friction.

Google collects user searches, smart speaker interactions, clicked results, and ads, favoring DuckDuckGo for privacy despite potential performance issues. Its index is over 100 million gigabytes, using machine learning to rank results by quality and usability. In 2022, Google ran almost 900,000 quality tests with independent raters. Critics like Megan Grey contend that semantic keyword matching reduces precision to widen content pools and increase ad auctions. Megan Grey, former DuckDuckGo VP, admits possible evidence misinterpretation but maintains Google manipulates Search to maximize ad revenue.

Danny Sullivan states that ad systems do not affect organic results (blue links); keyword matching connects people to ads, while a separate process matches organic results to queries using meaning matching. Conversely, Bing Chat failed to filter results for 'kids BMX bike green' under $200, returning only options over $300, and lacks functional follow-up questions despite an overhaul with generative AI. Global data creation grew from 9 ZB/year in 2013 to 120 ZB in 2023, shifting from static websites to live information nested in apps. The US faces an uphill battle proving Google broke the law to achieve its market status quo, while others gain insight into Google's market share usage. Wired removed an article on Google Search manipulation, though social sharing and coverage elsewhere show public willingness to accept foul play and suspicion of privacy invasion.

# See also

* [Apple defends Google Search deal in court: 'There wasn't a valid alternative'](apple-defends-google-search-deal-in-court-there-wasn-t-a.md) - Eddy Cue testified in US v. Google that Apple had no valid alternative to Google's search engine, negotiated the 2016 ISA with Sundar Pichai, and argued the deal prioritized user experience over economics.
* [Google antitrust case: key facts and Google's defense](google-antitrust-case-key-facts-and-google-s-defense.md) - Overview of the U.S. government's antitrust trial against Google, including CEO Sundar Pichai's testimony on default search engine deals, specific financial figures, and historical context regarding browser defaults.
* [Helena World Chronicle files antitrust suit against Google and Alphabet](helena-world-chronicle-files-antitrust-suit-against-google.md) - Arkansas publisher Helena World Chronicle filed a class action lawsuit in U.S. District Court in D.C. accusing Google and Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior under the Sherman Act, alleging they siphon off content, readers, and ad revenue through AI technologies like Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard, and older tools like the Knowledge Graph launched in May 2012.
